claim: Six rhesus monkeys performed a temporal-order judgement (TOJ) task with naturalistic videos.
source: We trained six rhesus monkeys with a temporal-order judgement (TOJ) task and collected 5000 TOJ trials. In each trial, the monkeys watched a naturalistic video of about 10 s comprising two across-context clips, and after a 2 s delay, performed TOJ between two frames from the video.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental design and number of subjects.

claim: Macaque monkeys demonstrate a non-linear, time-compressed forward memory replay mechanism.
source: The data are suggestive of a non-linear, time-compressed forward memory replay mechanism in the macaque.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a main finding from the experimental data.

claim: Monkeys cannot compress encoded video globally to skip over irrelevant information as effectively as humans.
source: In contrast with humans, such compression of replay is, however, not sophisticated enough to allow these monkeys to skip over irrelevant information by compressing the encoded video globally.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a comparative finding between species.

claim: Monkeys detect event contextual boundaries, which facilitates recall by increasing the rate of information accumulation.
source: We also reveal that the monkeys detect event contextual boundaries, and that such detection facilitates recall by increasing the rate of information accumulation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the experimental data.

claim: Non-human primates possess the ability to remember temporal relationships among events.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that non-human primates possess the ability to remember temporal relationships among events (Templer and Hampton, 2013; Gower, 1992; Charles et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Apes can remember movies based on the temporal order of scenes.
source: The apes can remember movies based on the temporal order of scenes (Morimura and Matsuzawa, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Apes can keep track of the past time of episodes.
source: keep track of the past time of episodes (Martin-Ordas et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Macaque monkeys possess serial and ordinal positions expertise for multi-item lists.
source: whereas macaque monkeys possess serial (Terrace et al., 2003) and ordinal positions expertise for multi-item lists (Chen et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Macaque monkeys are able to categorize sequences of fractal images by their ordinal number.
source: and are able to categorize sequences of fractal images by their ordinal number (Orlov et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Episodes can be replayed sequentially in humans on the basis of learned structures.
source: In the human literature, it has been shown that episodes can be replayed sequentially on the basis of learned structures (Liu et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Episodes can be replayed sequentially in humans on the basis of sensory information.
source: sensory information (Michelmann et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Episodes can be replayed sequentially in humans on the basis of pictorial content.
source: and pictorial content (Wimmer et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Memory replay in humans during cued-recall tasks proceeds in a forward manner and is temporally compressed.
source: Recent findings in rodents (Panoz-Brown et al., 2018) and in humans of memory replay during cued-recall tasks across fragments of video episodes are characterized, however, by replay that proceeds in a forward manner and is temporally compressed (Michelmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Memory replay in rodents during cued-recall tasks proceeds in a forward manner and is temporally compressed.
source: Recent findings in rodents (Panoz-Brown et al., 2018) and in humans of memory replay during cued-recall tasks across fragments of video episodes are characterized, however, by replay that proceeds in a forward manner and is temporally compressed (Michelmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Memory replay allows subjects to skip flexibly across sub-events.
source: A feature of this more sophisticated mechanism is that memory replay is a fluidic process that allows subjects to skip flexibly across sub-events (Michelmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All six monkeys learned to perform the temporal order judgement task with dynamic cinematic videos.
source: All six monkeys learned to perform the temporal order judgement task with dynamic cinematic videos as encoded content (Figure 1B left and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and Video 1 showing task performance.

claim: The six monkeys performed the task with a significantly above chance level with an overall accuracy of 67.9% ± 1.5%.
source: The six monkeys performed the task with a significantly above chance level with an overall accuracy of 67.9% ± 1.5% (mean ± SD).
evidence: This claim presents quantitative performance data from the experiment.

claim: Human participants performed the task on average at 92.7% ± 1.2%.
source: The human participants performed the task on average at 92.7% ± 1.2% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, left).
evidence: This claim presents quantitative performance data from the experiment with reference to a figure.

claim: There is a negative relationship between reciprocal latency and chosen frame location in all monkeys.
source: We found a negative relationship between reciprocal latency and chosen frame location in all monkeys (all p<0.001 ; Figure 1C and Table 1 upper panel)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: There is a negative relationship between reciprocal latency and temporal similarity in all monkeys.
source: and between reciprocal latency and temporal similarity (all p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 2 upper panel)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Monkeys are systemically faster in identifying frames that are located earlier in the video.
source: This suggests that the monkeys are systemically faster in identifying frames that are located earlier in the video.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative relationship between reciprocal latency and chosen frame location.

claim: Frames presented in Clip 1 were retrieved significantly faster than those experienced in Clip 2.
source: During TOJ retrieval, frames that were presented in Clip 1 (mean reaction time = 1.59 s) were retrieved significantly faster than those that were experienced in Clip 2 (mean reaction time = 1.88 s) (one-tailed t5 = −4.533; p=0.003; Cohen's d = −0.54; 95% CI: –infinity to −0.158 s; log(RT): one-tailed t5 = −6.473; p=6.558 × e−4; Cohen's d = −0.69; 95% CI: –infinity to −0.114 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of reaction time data.

claim: The replay of the video was conducted at a compressed speed.
source: Moreover, since the latency required to respond to the chosen frames is much smaller than the duration of the videos themselves, the replay of the video must have been conducted at a compressed speed (i.e., memory replay was faster than perception during video-watching).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing reaction times to video duration.

claim: The difference in reaction time between the very first frame and the last frame was averaged at 942 ms.
source: The difference in reaction time between the very first frame and the last frame was averaged at 942 ms (range: 468–1859 ms).
evidence: This claim presents quantitative data from the experiment.

claim: The compression factor during replay in monkeys is 10.61.
source: This is equivalent to 94.2 ms to scan through each second of the video, and corresponds to a compression factor of 10.61 during replay in these monkeys (compression factor for each monkey: Jupiter = 13.59, Mars = 7.39, Saturn = 14.80, Mercury = 21.37, Uranus = 17.78, Neptune = 5.38, see Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim presents calculated compression factors from the experimental data.

claim: The compression factor in humans is 13.7.
source: This is comparable to a compression factor of 13.7 observed in humans, corroborating the notion of forward replay and those findings in humans (Michelmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim cites a compression factor from previous human research.

claim: The monkeys' judgments are faster when responding to probe frames that are located in the earlier parts of the videos.
source: The results suggest that the monkeys' judgments are faster when responding to probe frames that are located in the earlier parts of the videos
evidence: This is a summary inference from the reaction time data.

claim: The search does not follow a linear function.
source: and they also illustrate that the search might not follow a linear function.
evidence: This is an inference from the non-linear patterns observed in the data.

claim: The non-linear relationship in the monkeys rules out alternative explanations in which the main effects simply result from positional effects.
source: This non-linear (quadratic and cubic) relationship in the monkeys is important because it rules out alternative explanations in which the main effects simply result from positional effects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the non-linear analysis results.

claim: The non-linear change in slope indicates that the monkeys might group the content according to the relational storyline structure.
source: Rather, the non-linear change in slope indicates that other factors are in play, and that the monkeys might group (or parse) the content according to the relational storyline structure (e.g., the two-clip video design), and do not merely recall the frames/items as of their ordinal positions in a fixed linear manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the non-linear patterns in the data.

claim: Human data fits best with the cubic model.
source: We found that the human data fits best, and only, with the cubic model (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: Humans might have treated the video and TOJ differently from the macaques.
source: suggesting that humans might have treated the video and TOJ differently from the macaques.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the different model fits between species.

claim: Monkeys performed TOJ of video episodes using a forward search of ordered elements in the mnemonic representation at the time of memory test with a non-linear, time-compressed function.
source: In summary, we found that our monkeys might have performed TOJ of video episodes using a forward search of ordered elements in the mnemonic representation at the time of memory test with a non-linear, time-compressed function.
evidence: This is a summary inference from multiple analyses.

claim: Human subjects showed a negative relationship between temporal similarity and reciprocal latency.
source: Showing a completely opposite pattern, regression analyses on human subjects showed a negative relationship between temporal similarity and reciprocal latency for all participants (all p<0.001, one subject with p=0.055, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 4 upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: The more similar the two frames to be judged, the longer time needed for humans to retrieve temporal order information.
source: These results imply that the more similar the two frames to be judged, the longer time needed for retrieve temporal order information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative relationship between temporal similarity and reciprocal latency in humans.

claim: There was no observable reciprocal latency/chosen frame location slope in the human data.
source: There was also no observable reciprocal latency/chosen frame location slope in the human data (if anything, it shows an opposite trend; see Figure 1D and Supplementary file 4 bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of human data with reference to figures.

claim: Humans can make use of the across-clip boundary to facilitate their TOJ.
source: It is clear that humans can make use of the across-clip boundary to facilitate their TOJ.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the accuracy data as a function of frame location.

claim: TOJ performance is better for frames taken from an across-context condition than for frames taken from a within-context condition in both the proportion of correct answers and RTs.
source: whereas we show that TOJ performance is better for frames taken from an across-context condition than for frames taken from a within-context condition in both the proportion of correct answers and RTs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by performance data with reference to a figure.

claim: Accuracy and response times are worse in TOJ for items that are separated by a boundary during encoding in paradigms using discrete images.
source: Specifically, it has been reported that accuracy and response times are worse in TOJ for items are that separated by a boundary during encoding in the literature (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014; Heusser et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The monkeys showed a mild numerical increase trend in inverse efficiency score across the four segments but this did not reach statistical significance.
source: The monkeys showed a mild numeral increase in inverse efficiency score across the four segments but this trend did not reach statistical significance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, left panel) [F (3, 20) = 0.10, p=0.96]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The increase in RT towards the end of the video did not contribute to better accuracy in monkeys.
source: suggesting that the increase in RT towards the end of the video did not contribute to better accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inverse efficiency score analysis.

claim: Humans showed a lower inverse efficiency score for the video parts immediately after a boundary.
source: By contrast, we found that the humans showed a lower inverse efficiency score for the video parts immediately after a boundary (bars 2 and 3 in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right panel) [F (3, 24) = 4.17, p=0.016, a post hoc test shows significant difference between bar 2 and bar 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The RT for TOJ between each segment of the video increases linearly according to their position in encoding in monkeys.
source: The RT for TOJ between each segment of the video increases linearly according to their position in encoding (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Monkey RT data showed significant correlation with the Strict forward model.
source: We tested these against a hypothetical 'Strict forward' model and found significant correlation with the Strict forward model (r = 0.66, p=0.009)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Monkey RT data did not show significant correlation with the Global compression model.
source: but not with the Global compression model (r = −0.16, p=0.802) (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Human RT data did not show significant correlation with the Strict forward model.
source: Contrarily, these correlational patterns with the Strict forward model are not observed in the human subjects (r = −0.11, p=0.703)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Human RT data showed a trend favoring the global compression model.
source: but rather we observe a trend favoring the global compression model instead (r = 0.39, p=0.069) (Figure 3B right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: The Spearman correlation values between the monkey's data and hypothetical RDMs reach an asymptote of around r = 0.8 as the offset parameter tends to zero.
source: The results show that the Spearman correlation values between the monkey's data and hypothetical RDMs reach an asymptote of around r = 0.8 as the offset parameter tends to zero
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis across different offset parameters.

claim: The correlation values only improve minimally with increasing offsets in monkeys.
source: and notably, that the correlation values only improve minimally with increasing offsets (Figure 4B, with each individual's RT RDM displayed as an inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The monkeys have processed the video as a holistic chunk of information rather than taking advantage of skipping the non-informative first clip.
source: These results suggest that the monkeys have processed the video as a holistic chunk of information rather than taking advantage of skipping the non-informative first clip when the two probe frames were in Clip 2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the offset parameter analysis.

claim: Human participants showed a completely opposite pattern from monkeys in the offset parameter analysis.
source: For comparison, we also tested human participant's data against each of these 11 hypothetical models and found a completely opposite pattern in the humans (Figure 4C, with each individual's RT RDM displayed as an inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The shift model is better than the swivel model for all six monkeys according to BIC.
source: Using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) as an index of model comparison, the results consistently indicate that the shift model is better than the swivel model for all six monkeys [range of ΔBIC = (14.57, 300.07); Supplementary file 3, see section 'Model comparison' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: Contextual changes do not alter the judgement threshold for decisions in monkeys.
source: These results further indicate that contextual changes do not alter the judgement threshold for decisions (providing no evidence for a swivel pattern).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the LATER model comparison.

claim: The shift pattern is not seen in the human participants.
source: By contrast, this pattern is not seen in the human participants (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Monkeys accumulate information for memory decisions at a faster rate when the frames were extracted from two different clips than when the frames were extracted from the same-context clip.
source: Within a drift diffusion model framework, the results suggest that monkeys accumulate information for memory decisions at a faster rate when the frames were extracted from two different clips than when the frames were extracted from the same-context clip.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the LATER model results within a drift diffusion framework.

claim: Monkeys' RT was significantly faster when the probe frame was located earlier in the video in within-context trials.
source: The within-context GLM shows that monkeys' RT was indeed significantly faster when the probe frame was located earlier in the video, p<0.001 (or in equivalent terms, when two frames were temporally closer, p=0.004), confirming our main finding that the monkeys might have adopted a forward scanning strategy for information retrieval (Figure 6A, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: In across-context trials, there was no significant effect of the chosen frame location on RT in monkeys.
source: By contrast, the across-context GLM shows that there was no significant effect of the chosen frame location on RT.
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis.

claim: The monkeys retrieve their memories significantly faster for probe frames that are contextually (or perceptually) distinct in across-context trials.
source: Rather, the monkeys retrieve their memories significantly faster for probe frames that are contextually (or perceptually) distinct, p=0.004 (Figure 6A , right).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: No obvious increase in performance was observed over the course of testing days in the experiment for either monkeys or humans.
source: Considering that the monkeys performed a larger number of trials than the human participants (5000 vs. 2000 trials), we plotted the accuracy data for each testing day for each monkey (and for humans too, Figure 7) and observed no apparent increase in performance over the course of the 50 testing days.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of performance over time with reference to a figure.

claim: The main effects reported are unlikely to be attributable to behavioral or strategic changes over the course of main experiment.
source: We therefore deem the main effects reported here as unlikely to be attributable to behavioral or strategic changes over the course of main experiment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of performance changes over time and extensive training.

claim: Macaques can replay their memory in a serial forward manner.
source: Taking advantage of the latency data obtained during TOJ on naturalistic materials, we provide new behavioral evidence in support of the hypothesis proposed by Gower, 1992 that the monkeys can replay their memory in a serial forward manner.
evidence: This claim synthesizes the experimental findings with reference to a previous hypothesis.

claim: Both humans and macaques execute retrieval with forward replay with a comparable compression factor.
source: Notwithstanding task differences, both humans and macaques execute retrieval with forward replay with a comparable compression factor (factors of ~11 in macaques vs. ~13 in humans, Michelmann et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim compares findings across species with reference to previous research.

claim: The RT patterns are independent of retrieval success in both humans and macaques.
source: Another cross-species similarity rests on the observation that the RT patterns are independent of retrieval success.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of RT patterns across correct and incorrect trials.

claim: TOJ task-specific BOLD activation and behavioral RT patterns are independent of retrieval accuracy in humans.
source: We have previously showed in analogous TOJ paradigms in humans that TOJ task-specific BOLD activation and behavioral RT patterns are independent of retrieval accuracy (Kwok et al., 2012; Kwok and Macaluso, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: The latency results point towards some 'search' or replay processes.
source: At present, the latency results probably also point towards some 'search' or replay processes
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the latency data patterns.

claim: Incorrect responses are likely to be caused by memory noises injected during encoding and/or during delay maintenance.
source: and any ultimate incorrect responses are thus likely to be caused by memory noises injected during encoding and/or during delay maintenance.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the source of errors.

claim: Humans can do both local and global compression, whereas monkeys are not able to attain global compression.
source: Despite the cross-species similarity, our revelation of a critical discrepancy between humans and macaques carries an important theoretical implication: humans can do both local and global compression, whereas monkeys are not able to attain global compression.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the comparative analyses between species.

claim: Mental time travel is not all-or-none.
source: The implication is that mental time travel is not all-or-none.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference drawn from the species differences.

claim: There could be multiple layers underpinning the concept of mental time travel.
source: There could be multiple layers underpinning the concept of mental time travel, which entail the ability to relive the past (Suddendorf et al., 2009; Tulving, 1985) and skipping over unimportant information (Michelmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference with support from citations.

claim: The ability to skip over unimportant information allows humans to recall memories flexibly far into the past.
source: The latter aspect allows humans to recall our memories flexibly far into our past and suggest powerful computational efficiencies that may facilitate memory storage and recall.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of global compression.

claim: It remains unknown how far back in time monkeys can replay their memories.
source: It thus remains unknown how far back in time monkeys can replay their memories.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in current knowledge.

claim: Humans can spontaneously replay experience on the basis of learned structures.
source: It has been shown recently that humans can spontaneously replay experience on the basis of learned structures, with fast structural generalization to new experiences facilitated by representing structural information in a format that is independent of its sensory consequences (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The lack of global compression in the monkeys implies that they might not be able to use factorized representations to allow components to be recombined in more ways than were experienced.
source: The lack of global compression in the monkeys of their video experience implies that the monkeys might not be able to use factorized representations to allow components to be recombined in more ways than were experienced (Behrens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings with reference to a theoretical framework.

claim: Neither the number of intervening frames nor the passage of time per se determines the RT pattern.
source: However, by establishing that neither the number of intervening frames nor the passage of time per se determines the RT pattern (probably a mixed effect resultant from a combination of both), we ruled out order or positional memory as the underlying mechanism supporting TOJ in this task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analyses ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Replay is a neural phenomenon supported by the activity of individual neurons and implicates the offline reactivation of sequences of hippocampal place cells.
source: Although we have argued for the presence of replay-like patterns in the monkey during TOJ, we are aware that replay is a neural phenomenon supported by the activity of individual neurons and that implicates the offline reactivation of sequences of hippocampal place cells that reflect past and future trajectories (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Jadhav et al., 2012; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural replay.

claim: In rodent research, replay has been linked to sharp wave-ripples in the hippocampal formation.
source: On the one hand, in rodent research, replay has been linked to sharp wave-ripples in the hippocampal formation (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent MEG studies on humans' replay have implicated several cortical areas such as the occipito-parietal cortex, the vmPFC, and the visual cortex, in addition to the MTL including the hippocampus.
source: On the other hand, recent MEG studies on humans' replay have implicated several cortical areas such as the occipito-parietal cortex (Michelmann et al., 2016), the vmPFC (Liu et al., 2019), and the visual cortex (Wimmer et al., 2019), in addition to the MTL including the hippocampus (Liu et al., 2019; Wimmer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Replay may be coordinated between the hippocampus and neocortical areas.
source: These observations, made under simultaneous whole-brain recordings in humans, are in line with the idea that replay may be coordinated between the hippocampus and neocortical areas (Ji and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most rodent studies on replay focus on spontaneous replay patterns at rest, during sleep, or during a task-free state.
source: A further caveat is that although most of the rodents studies on replay focus on spontaneous replay patterns at rest (Liu et al., 2019), during sleep (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Louie and Wilson, 2001) or during a task-free state (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The monkeys perform their replay-like recall of the videos as an effortful operation to solve a TOJ task.
source: our monkeys perform their replay-like recall of the videos as an effortful operation to solve a TOJ task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The combined results constitute a novel connection between various kinds of replay-like behaviors that are shared between rodents and humans.
source: Our combined results thus constitute a novel connection between various kinds of replay-like behaviors that are shared between rodents and humans, and provide a primate model for anatomical investigation.
evidence: This is an inference about the significance of the findings.

claim: The monkeys are able to detect contextual changes to facilitate TOJ.
source: We observed one further interesting phenomenon here, which is that the monkeys are able to detect contextual changes to facilitate TOJ.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the across-context vs within-context performance differences.

claim: The expedited TOJ in across-context condition was facilitated by contextual details, which results in an increased rate of rise of signal towards memory decision in a drift-diffusion process.
source: We show that the expedited TOJ in across-context condition was facilitated by contextual details, which in turn results in an increased rate of rise of signal towards memory decision in a drift-diffusion process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the LATER model results.

claim: Contextual changes lead to segmentation of ongoing information in humans.
source: Humans studies show that contextual changes lead to segmentation of ongoing information (Magliano et al., 2001; Hard et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results provide evidence consistent with event segmentation in the macaque monkeys.
source: Our results provide evidence consistent with event segmentation in the macaque monkeys
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the boundary detection findings.

claim: The monkeys might be capable of parsing the footage using contextual information.
source: and imply that these monkeys might be capable of parsing the footage using contextual information, akin to what has been shown in humans (DuBrow and Davachi, 2013; Sols et al., 2017; Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011; Kwok and Macaluso, 2015b) and rodents (Panoz-Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings with reference to previous research.

claim: Six male rhesus macaques with a mean age of 3.5 years participated in this study.
source: Six male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) (5.49 ± 0.5 kg) with a mean age of 3.5 years at the start of testing participated in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the subjects.

claim: Seven human participants with mean age 19.57 ± 1.13 took part in the experiment.
source: Seven participants (mean age = 19.57 ± 1.13, 6 female) took part in the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the subjects.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and the University Committee on Human Research Protection at East China Normal University.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (permission code: M020150902 and M020150902-2018) and the University Committee on Human Research Protection (permission code: HR 023–2017) at East China Normal University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Trials with RT longer than 10 s (1.45%) or shorter than 0.7 s (2.47%) were excluded from the analyses.
source: Trials with RT longer than 10 s (1.45%) or shorter than 0.7 s (2.47%) were excluded from the analyses.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Both correct and incorrect trials were entered for all analyses.
source: Both correct and incorrect trials were entered for all analyses.
evidence: This describes the data inclusion criteria.
